title: Practice Set 10 — Spark SQL: The SQL Interface
description: Apply Spark SQL to NordGrid's data: register views, write SQL queries with joins and aggregations, build multi-step analytics with CTEs, mix SQL and DataFrame operations, and construct a complete hybrid Bronze-Silver-Gold pipeline that uses every module in the course.

datasets.description: NordGrid Silver-quality meter readings. 125 rows: 30 meters × 4 dates + 5 null-reading rows from meters M-0031 to M-0035. Evenly distributed across 4 regions.
NordGrid meter reference table. 35 rows: M-0001 to M-0030 (matched) + M-0036 to M-0040 (unreported). Includes customer_type and substation_id.

tasks.title: Register Views and Query NordGrid Readings with SQL

description.context: NordGrid's analysts use SQL for ad-hoc exploration of the Silver meter readings. Before they can write SQL queries, the DataFrame must be registered as a temporary view. The analyst wants a quick summary: total consumption and reading count per region, ordered by total consumption descending.
description.task: Read PS10_data_readings.csv (header=True, inferSchema=True). Register the DataFrame as a temporary view called 'readings'. Then use spark.sql() to write a SQL query that: filters out null daily_kw, groups by region, computes SUM(daily_kw) as total_kw and COUNT(*) as reading_count, and orders by total_kw descending. Store the SQL result in a variable called regional_sql.
description.validationHint: regional_sql should have 4 rows (one per region). The query filters nulls using WHERE daily_kw IS NOT NULL, so only the 120 non-null rows are aggregated.

tasks.partialCredit: 4 independent assertions. Each passed assertion earns 1/4 credit.

tasks.title: Write a Multi-Table SQL Join

description.context: NordGrid's billing team needs a report that combines meter readings with customer type and substation name. This requires joining three tables: readings → meters (on meter_id) → substations (on substation_id). The analyst writes the entire query in SQL rather than chaining DataFrame joins.
description.task: Read all three CSVs and register them as views: 'readings', 'meters', and 'substations'. Write a SQL query that inner-joins all three tables, filters to non-null daily_kw, and selects meter_id, daily_kw, date, region, customer_type, and substation_name. Store the result in a variable called enriched_sql.
description.validationHint: The inner join keeps only meters present in all three tables. Meters M-0031 to M-0035 (in readings but not in meters ref) are dropped. The result should have 120 rows (30 meters × 4 dates, minus the 5 null rows that also get filtered).

tasks.title: Build a CTE-Based Analytics Report

description.context: NordGrid's regulatory team needs a regional consumption report built with CTEs for clarity. The report must: (1) filter to valid (non-null, positive) readings, (2) aggregate by region to compute total_kw, avg_kw, and reading_count, and (3) add a compliance_status column: 'ABOVE_THRESHOLD' if avg_kw > 2000, 'WITHIN_LIMIT' otherwise. Each step should be a named CTE.
description.task: Register the readings DataFrame as a view. Write a single spark.sql() query with two CTEs: the first CTE called 'valid_readings' filters out null and non-positive daily_kw; the second CTE called 'regional_summary' aggregates by region. The final SELECT adds the compliance_status using CASE WHEN. Store the result in a variable called compliance_report.
description.validationHint: The report should have 4 rows. ROUND the avg_kw to 1 decimal. The compliance_status should be based on the avg_kw of each region.

description.context: Spark's DataFrame API and SQL interface compile to the SAME logical plan via Catalyst. Performance is identical; the choice is purely about readability. Two practical rules to remember: (1) spark.sql() requires a REGISTERED VIEW — calling SELECT FROM readings without first calling createOrReplaceTempView('readings') raises AnalysisException because Spark does not auto-discover DataFrames. (2) Temporary views are SESSION-SCOPED — a view registered in one SparkSession is invisible to another. createGlobalTempView is the cross-session variant (accessed via global_temp.viewname). spark.sql() returns a regular DataFrame, so you can chain .filter, .withColumn, .write on its result and Catalyst will optimize the combined plan.
description.task: Predict the behavior in four mixed-API scenarios.
description.validationHint: SQL and DataFrame API compile to the same execution plan via Catalyst. Views are session-scoped and disappear when the session stops.

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Four scenarios mixing DataFrame API and SQL; predict each outcome.

fields.label: df.filter(col('daily_kw') > 2000).groupBy('region').agg(count('*').alias('cnt')) and spark.sql("SELECT region, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM readings WHERE daily_kw > 2000 GROUP BY region") — do they produce the same results?
options: Yes — both compile to the SAME logical and physical plan via Catalyst, so the result rows and performance are identical; the choice is purely about readability.
No — SQL is faster because it bypasses Python overhead and runs directly in the JVM.
No — the DataFrame API treats nulls differently than SQL because col-based comparisons use Pythonic truthiness.
It depends on the data size — both work for small data but produce different plans on large data.
fields.correctAnswer: Yes — both compile to the SAME logical and physical plan via Catalyst, so the result rows and performance are identical; the choice is purely about readability.
fields.rationale: Catalyst is the unifying layer: it parses SQL strings into the same logical plan that DataFrame chains build directly. Both go through identical optimization and execution. The most common Junior confusion is assuming SQL is faster (it 'looks like database code'); in reality the DataFrame API is just a Python builder for the same plan SQL parses to.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Both run in the JVM after Catalyst translation; Python overhead is a one-time plan-construction cost.

Option C: Null handling is unified across SQL and DataFrame.

Option D: Plan equivalence is not data-size dependent.

fields.label: An engineer calls spark.sql("SELECT * FROM readings") without first calling createOrReplaceTempView('readings'). What happens?
options: Spark scans the workspace for any DataFrame variable named 'readings' and auto-registers it as a view; the query then runs successfully.
Spark raises an AnalysisException: Table or view not found: readings; you MUST register the DataFrame as a view before SQL can reference it.
Spark returns an empty DataFrame because the missing view is treated as an empty source.
Spark reads from a file named 'readings' in the working directory as a fallback.
fields.correctAnswer: Spark raises an AnalysisException: Table or view not found: readings; you MUST register the DataFrame as a view before SQL can reference it.
fields.rationale: spark.sql() resolves names against the catalog (registered views, tables, databases). DataFrame Python variables are NOT in the catalog. The fix is df.createOrReplaceTempView('readings') or df.createTempView('readings'). The most common Junior confusion is expecting Spark to introspect Python scope; in fact spark.sql is database-style — names must be registered explicitly.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Spark does not introspect Python variables; the catalog is explicit.

Option C: Missing tables raise errors, not silent empties.

Option D: spark.sql does not look at filesystem paths.

fields.label: A temporary view is registered in Session A. Can Session B (a different SparkSession) access this view?
options: Yes — temporary views live on the cluster and are shared across all sessions automatically.
No — temporary views are SESSION-SCOPED; they live only in the catalog of the session that created them. createGlobalTempView() is the cross-session alternative (accessed as global_temp.viewname).
Yes — if both sessions are created with the same appName the catalog is shared.
Only if Session B was created with .enableHiveSupport(); otherwise temp views are private.
fields.correctAnswer: No — temporary views are SESSION-SCOPED; they live only in the catalog of the session that created them. createGlobalTempView() is the cross-session alternative (accessed as global_temp.viewname).
fields.rationale: Each SparkSession has its own catalog of temporary views. createGlobalTempView puts views in a special global_temp database accessible across sessions in the same Spark application. The most common Junior confusion is treating temp views as cluster-wide; in reality they are session-private, which is intentional — it prevents one user's exploration from polluting another's catalog.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Temp views are session-private by design.

Option C: appName is just a label; it does not create catalog sharing.

Option D: enableHiveSupport gives access to a Hive metastore, not cross-session temp views.

fields.label: spark.sql() returns a DataFrame. Can you call .withColumn(), .filter(), and .write.parquet() on the result?
options: No — DataFrames returned by spark.sql() are READ-ONLY snapshots; you must re-register them as a view to apply further transformations.
Yes — spark.sql() returns a standard DataFrame indistinguishable from one built via the DataFrame API; you can chain any DataFrame methods on it and Catalyst optimizes the combined plan.
Only if you call .toDataFrame() on the SQL result first to convert it from a RowBag back to a DataFrame.
Yes, but the operations will run slower because mixing SQL and DataFrame chains forces Catalyst to recompile.
fields.correctAnswer: Yes — spark.sql() returns a standard DataFrame indistinguishable from one built via the DataFrame API; you can chain any DataFrame methods on it and Catalyst optimizes the combined plan.
fields.rationale: There is exactly ONE DataFrame type in Spark; the SQL interface is just another way to build one. The mixed pattern (SQL for joins/aggregations, DataFrame chain for I/O and final tweaks) is the canonical hybrid pipeline. The most common Junior confusion is treating SQL as a separate world; in reality SQL is just sugar over DataFrame plan construction.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: SQL results are full DataFrames, mutable via the API like any other.

Option C: No 'toDataFrame' method exists; the result IS a DataFrame.

Option D: Mixing does not slow down anything; Catalyst optimizes one combined plan.

tasks.title: Choose SQL vs DataFrame API for Each Pipeline Stage

description.context: NordGrid's convention picks the right interface per pipeline stage. DATAFRAME API for ETL: file I/O (spark.read/write), type casting, string cleaning, simple filters — every method maps to one transformation, and chaining reads top-to-bottom like a recipe. SQL for ANALYTICS: multi-table joins, aggregations with GROUP BY, CASE WHEN tiers, CTEs for stepwise logic — SQL is more readable when the query has multiple tables and aggregations. HYBRID for production: DataFrame API loads files and writes outputs, then registers views and runs SQL for the analytical core. Catalog discovery is via spark.catalog.listTables() (returns registered views and tables in the current database).
description.task: Pick the right interface for each scenario.
description.validationHint: The DataFrame API is strongest for step-by-step ETL. SQL is strongest for complex multi-table analytics. Hybrid uses each where it shines.

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Four pipeline stages from NordGrid's daily run; pick the right interface for each.

fields.label: Reading a messy CSV, casting types, trimming strings, filtering nulls, and writing Parquet. Which interface?
options: SQL — express the whole flow as CREATE TABLE AS SELECT, with type casts and string functions inline.
DataFrame API — step-by-step ETL with spark.read.csv, withColumn for casting, filter for nulls, and write.parquet for output. The method-chain reads as a linear recipe.
Either is equally suited; the team should pick whichever interface they prefer for ETL.
Hybrid — SQL for reading the file, DataFrame for the transformations and write.
fields.correctAnswer: DataFrame API — step-by-step ETL with spark.read.csv, withColumn for casting, filter for nulls, and write.parquet for output. The method-chain reads as a linear recipe.
fields.rationale: ETL — file I/O, casting, string cleaning, write — is the DataFrame API's sweet spot. Each step maps to a method call, the chain reads top-to-bottom, and file paths/options are first-class arguments. SQL can do the same but requires CREATE TABLE syntax with format options that feels cumbersome for I/O. The most common Junior confusion is mixing interfaces unnecessarily; ETL is one thing, and one interface (DataFrame) handles it cleanly.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: CTAS works but is awkward for messy file I/O.

Option C: They are not equal for ETL; DataFrame is clearly better.

Option D: SQL is not the right tool for file reads with options.

fields.label: Joining 3 tables, aggregating with GROUP BY, applying CASE WHEN for tiered pricing, and pivoting by region. Which interface?
options: DataFrame API — chain df1.join(df2).join(df3).groupBy().agg().withColumn().pivot(); the chain is verbose but correct.
SQL — multi-table joins with GROUP BY, CASE WHEN, and PIVOT are exactly what SQL was designed for. The query reads as one declarative statement instead of a long Python chain.
Python UDF — the tiered pricing logic requires Python code that SQL cannot express.
Pandas — convert to Pandas after loading, since complex analytics are easier in Pandas.
fields.correctAnswer: SQL — multi-table joins with GROUP BY, CASE WHEN, and PIVOT are exactly what SQL was designed for. The query reads as one declarative statement instead of a long Python chain.
fields.rationale: SQL is the better READABILITY choice for multi-table analytics. The DataFrame API can do everything SQL does, but a long .join().join().groupBy().agg().pivot() chain is harder to scan than a single SELECT with FROM, JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, and CASE WHEN. The most common Junior confusion is preferring 'pythonic' chains for analytics; in production, analytics queries are usually written in SQL precisely because of readability.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Works but harder to read than SQL.

Option C: CASE WHEN is built-in SQL; no UDF needed.

Option D: Pandas defeats Spark's distribution and crashes on large data.

fields.label: A Gold pipeline loads Silver Parquet with DataFrame API, then needs a complex aggregation with 3 CTEs. Which approach for the aggregation?
options: Rewrite the entire pipeline in SQL including the file read using CREATE TABLE USING parquet OPTIONS().
Use DataFrame API for loading and writing (its strength), then createOrReplaceTempView and write the 3-CTE aggregation in SQL (SQL's strength). This is the canonical hybrid pattern.
Use DataFrame API for everything — CTEs translate to chained sub-DataFrames stored in intermediate variables.
Use SQL for loading and aggregation; spark.sql can read Parquet directly via SELECT * FROM parquet.`/path/`.
fields.correctAnswer: Use DataFrame API for loading and writing (its strength), then createOrReplaceTempView and write the 3-CTE aggregation in SQL (SQL's strength). This is the canonical hybrid pattern.
fields.rationale: Hybrid is the production-grade default: DataFrame for I/O and structural plumbing, SQL for analytical core. CTEs especially benefit from SQL because each CTE has a NAME and the chain of CTEs reads as a top-down logical pipeline. The most common Junior confusion is treating one interface as 'the right one'; in reality each is a tool optimized for different shapes of work.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: All-SQL adds complexity for the I/O parts.

Option C: Multi-CTE chains are more readable in SQL than as Python intermediate variables.

Option D: spark.sql can read parquet paths but is not the convention for production loading.

fields.label: An analyst writes SQL queries on Gold tables for ad-hoc exploration. Which catalog operation helps them discover available views?
options: spark.conf.get('spark.sql.views') — Spark exposes the view list as a configuration property.
spark.catalog.listTables() — the catalog API returns every registered table and view in the current database with name, type, and description.
spark.sql('SHOW DATABASES') — listing databases is the standard discovery path.
spark.read.format('catalog').load() — load the catalog as a DataFrame.
fields.correctAnswer: spark.catalog.listTables() — the catalog API returns every registered table and view in the current database with name, type, and description.
fields.rationale: spark.catalog.listTables() is the canonical discovery method. It returns a list of Table objects with name, database, type ('TEMPORARY' / 'MANAGED' / 'EXTERNAL'), and isTemporary flag. The SQL equivalent is spark.sql('SHOW TABLES'). The most common Junior confusion is reaching for a config or filesystem path; the catalog API is the right tool because views are catalog metadata, not files.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: No such config property exists.

Option C: Lists databases, not tables/views within a database.

Option D: No 'catalog' read format exists.

tasks.title: Build NordGrid's Capstone Hybrid Pipeline

description.context: This is the capstone task of the junior-level PySpark track. NordGrid's complete daily pipeline uses the DataFrame API for ETL and SQL for Gold-layer analytics. The pipeline: reads raw readings, cleans them (DataFrame API), writes Silver Parquet, registers Silver as a view, joins with reference tables in SQL, aggregates with a CTE, and writes the Gold result.
description.task: Write a hybrid pipeline: (1) Read PS10_data_readings.csv with inferSchema=True; (2) Filter out null and non-positive daily_kw using DataFrame API; (3) Register the cleaned DataFrame as view 'silver_readings'; (4) Read meters ref and substations CSVs, register as views 'meters' and 'substations'; (5) Write a SQL query with a CTE: the CTE 'enriched' joins silver_readings → meters → substations on the appropriate keys; the final SELECT aggregates from 'enriched' by region to produce total_kw (SUM), avg_kw (ROUND(AVG, 1)), and reading_count (COUNT). Store the result in a variable called gold.
description.validationHint: The cleaned readings should have ~120 rows (null and non-positive removed). The inner joins drop unmatched meters. Gold should have 4 rows with region, total_kw, avg_kw, reading_count.

tasks.partialCredit: 6 independent assertions. Each passed assertion earns 1/6 credit.

conceptsCombined: DataFrame API for reading CSV and filtering (Modules 3-4, 8)
SQL aggregation with GROUP BY (Lesson 2, Module 6)
SQL functions: SUM, AVG, ROUND, COUNT (Lesson 7)
Hybrid pipeline pattern: DataFrame ETL + SQL analytics (Lesson 5, 9)
synthesisNotes.rationale: This capstone task uses the hybrid pattern from Lessons 5 and 9: DataFrame API handles file I/O and data cleaning (its strength), then SQL handles multi-table joins with aggregation (its strength). The CTE structures the SQL into readable steps. This is the exact pipeline pattern NordGrid uses in production and draws skills from every module in the course: reading (M8), filtering (M4), view registration (M10), SQL joins (M7+M10), aggregation (M6+M10), and CTEs (M10).
